blocks.text: A segment tree is a binary tree where each node stores an aggregate over a range of the array, and leaves store individual elements. This topic focuses specifically on SUM as the aggregate function, the most common and natural first aggregate to learn, and goes deep on the nuances specific to sum queries.

Sum works as a segment tree aggregate because it is ASSOCIATIVE: a parent's sum is simply the sum of its two children's sums. This associativity property is exactly what segment trees require of ANY aggregate function they support, min and max (covered in a sibling topic) also work because they are associative too, but something like median would not.

blocks.caption: Each internal node stores the sum of its two children. Leaves store individual array elements.

blocks.text: Recursively build both children first, then set a node's sum to leftChild.sum plus rightChild.sum. This bottom up construction is O(n) total despite looking like it might cost more, because the total work across all levels sums to a geometric series bounded by O(n), the same reasoning used for building a heap.

blocks.caption: Every recursive call falls into one of three cases based on how the node's range relates to the query range.

blocks.text: Given a query range [l, r], compare it against the current node's range [nodeL, nodeR]. If the node's range is completely OUTSIDE the query range, return 0, the identity element for sum, and stop. If the node's range is completely INSIDE the query range, return the node's precomputed sum directly without recursing further. Otherwise, a partial overlap, recurse into both children and add their results.

Querying the range [1,6] on an 8 element array's segment tree: the root [0,7] partially overlaps [1,6], so recurse into both children. [0,3] partially overlaps [1,6] too, recurse further, while [4,7] partially overlaps as well, recurse further. Eventually [2,3] and [4,5] are found to be COMPLETELY INSIDE [1,6], so their cached sums are returned directly without any further recursion, while [0,1] and [6,7] are only PARTIALLY inside, requiring one more level of recursion down to individual leaves 1, and 6 respectively.
This mix of skipped nodes, directly used nodes, and partially recursed nodes is exactly what keeps the total work at O(log n) despite the tree containing O(n) total nodes.

A point update propagates up: change a leaf's value, then walk back up updating each ancestor's sum as the sum of its two children. This is covered in more general depth in the introduction topic, the specific detail worth noting here is simply that the combine step is addition, matching the build and query logic above.

Build is O(n), query is O(log n), point update is O(log n). Query is O(log n) despite the tree having O(n) nodes because the recursion only ever explores O(log n) boundary nodes that have partial overlap, plus a bounded number of fully inside nodes at each level, the total work per level is constant, and there are O(log n) levels.

content.title: 7. Segment Tree vs Fenwick Tree for Sum

blocks.content: {"headers":["","Segment Tree","Fenwick Tree"],"rows":[["Memory","Roughly 4n","Roughly n"],["Supported aggregates","Any associative operation, sum, min, max, gcd, etc","Only invertible operations like sum"],["Code complexity","Slightly more code, explicit recursion","Simpler, shorter, iterative lowbit walks"],["Query and update cost","O(log n) both","O(log n) both"]]}

blocks.text: For sum specifically, a Fenwick tree is usually the simpler and more memory efficient choice, a segment tree earns its extra complexity when the aggregate is NOT a sum, like min, max, or gcd, which a Fenwick tree cannot support directly since its technique relies on being able to subtract out contributions.

Returning the wrong identity element for the completely outside case: for sum it must be 0, using a different identity like infinity (correct for a min segment tree) would be wrong for sum specifically.

Recursing further even when a node's range is fully inside the query range: this is not incorrect, since the recursion would still eventually reach the same leaves and produce the right answer, but it defeats the entire purpose of the O(log n) bound, the cached sum should be returned immediately instead.

Range Sum Query Mutable is the direct application, notably solvable with EITHER a Fenwick tree or a segment tree, worth knowing both and understanding the tradeoffs from the comparison table above when asked which to choose.
